title: Numbers, quantity and order
intro: Read plate 5 alongside this unit. Several numerals are grouped into single entries because they are learned as a run. Note that Spanish reverses the English punctuation: 1.500 is one and a half thousand, and 3,5 is three and a half.

entries.note: uno stands alone, un goes before a masculine noun, una before a feminine one. The same shortening hits veintiún and treinta y un.

ex.es: Necesito un boleto y una maleta.
ex.en: I need a ticket and a suitcase.
There are five of us in the family.

ex.es: El tren sale a las diez.

entries.note: These five are irregular and simply have to be learned. From sixteen the pattern becomes regular.
Literally ten-and-six, written as one word. dieciséis carries an accent; the others do not.

ex.en: I worked there for eighteen months.

entries.note: The twenties are one word; from thirty on they split into three: treinta y uno.
sesenta and setenta differ by one letter and are easy to confuse when spoken quickly.
cien exactly, and before a noun or before mil. ciento only when something follows: ciento cinco.

ex.es: Hay cien personas en la sala.
ex.en: There are a hundred people in the room.
I paid a hundred and twenty pesos.

entries.note: Never un mil — mil stands alone. But un millón takes de before a noun: un millón de personas.

ex.es: El vuelo cuesta mil quinientos pesos.
ex.en: The flight costs fifteen hundred pesos.

ex.es: La ciudad tiene dos millones de habitantes.
ex.en: The city has two million inhabitants.
What shoe size do you take?

entries.note: primero and tercero drop the -o before a masculine noun: el primer día, el tercer piso.

ex.en: I live on the first floor.
Did you read her latest book?

entries.note: medio agrees with its noun — media hora. la mitad is the thing itself, and takes de.

ex.es: Me comí la mitad del pastel.

entries.note: As adjectives they agree: muchas casas, pocos días. As adverbs they never change: trabaja mucho.

ex.en: There are a lot of options.

entries.note: todo el día is all day; todos los días is every day. One letter, two different meanings.
Both shorten before a masculine noun: algún día, ningún problema. ninguno needs no before the verb if it follows it.
Never changes form, and is always followed by a singular noun: cada persona.
Takes no article: otro café, never un otro café. That un is the commonest mistake English speakers make with it.

ex.en: Could you bring me another coffee, please?
